n151364091: Town and Country has a name that tells you its plan. Back in eighteen eighty-six this was a farming area called Altheim. In nineteen fifty it became a tiny village of just one hundred sixty-two people, and the idea was to keep a mix of town and country, homes tucked between woods and fields. Today it's one of the wealthiest cities in Missouri, with big homes on leafy lots, and it's also home to Missouri Baptist Medical Center. But the biggest news here was about golf. The famous Bellerive Country Club is in Town and Country, and it has hosted the U.S. Open in nineteen sixty-five and the PGA Championship twice. In August twenty eighteen, the hundredth PGA Championship came here, and Brooks Koepka won with a record-setting score, holding off Tiger Woods, who shot a sixty-four on the last day, his best ever final round in a major. The crowds' roars could be heard across these hills. So if anyone spots a golf course, passengers, give it a respectful wave.
n569768151: Chesterfield is a young city with an old story. It grew out of farmland in west St. Louis County and only became a city in nineteen eighty-eight. Just five years later came the news nobody here forgets. On July thirtieth, nineteen ninety-three, during the Great Flood, the Missouri River burst through the Monarch Levee, and the whole Chesterfield Valley, once nicknamed Gumbo Flats, filled with more than eight feet of muddy water. The city came back bigger, with higher levees and one of the largest strip malls in America. Now for the fun part: Faust Park. It has the Butterfly House, run by the Missouri Botanical Garden, where thousands of butterflies flutter around you, plus the historic St. Louis Carousel and a little historic village. And it's home to Thornhill, built in eighteen nineteen, the oldest governor's home still standing in Missouri. It belonged to Frederick Bates, Missouri's second governor, whose brother Edward Bates became Abraham Lincoln's Attorney General.
n6281417974: Weldon Spring is named for John Weldon, a frontiersman who settled beside a spring here on a Spanish land grant back in the seventeen-nineties, when this was still Spanish territory. The town itself was laid out in the eighteen-hundreds. Then came the big twist. In World War Two the Army moved out three little towns, Howell, Hamburg and Toonerville, and built what was called the largest explosives factory in the United States, making TNT. In nineteen fifty-five the Atomic Energy Commission added a uranium processing plant. The cleanup made national news and took years; in two thousand one all the waste was sealed inside a giant rock-covered hill, seventy-five feet tall and forty-one acres wide. Today that's the famous attraction: you can climb the stairs to the top for the view, and visit the interpretive center that opened in a new building in twenty twenty-two. Around it, the old factory land is now the Busch and Weldon Spring conservation areas, with lakes, deer and the Katy Trail along the Missouri River.
